headline: Sequence-scale computation infers microbial traits, host links, and viral origins
label: Microbial Genomic Inference Methods
summary: Large sequence collections now let computational models link microbial and viral genomes to host disease, taxonomy, gene order, and virus-likeness.
synthesis: The common thread is inference of microbial and viral properties directly from genome and metagenome-scale sequence data. Reconstructed phage genomes from 9,141 human gut metagenomes yield 3,794 endolysins with modular domain architectures, while annotation-free V-scores and VL-scores quantify virus-likeness of protein families and genomes. Whole-proteome ESM-2 embeddings of 21,657 foodborne bacterial genomes recover taxonomy and support geometry-based triage. PanBART, a transformer trained on gene content and gene order in E. coli and S. pneumoniae, targets genomic surveillance tasks. At the population level, harmonised whole-genome sequencing of 3,418 STEC isolates from 11 European countries examines population structure and host-disease associations. What is new is the shift toward learned representations of whole genomes and proteomes, alongside population-scale interpretation tied to host features. The items are heterogeneous, so this reflects the dominant thread rather than a shared method.
